# Cypress Monorepo — AGENTS.md

## Overview

Cypress is an open-source end-to-end and component testing framework for the modern web. This monorepo ships the Cypress desktop application and CLI (`cypress`), the JavaScript driver that runs tests in the browser, the Electron-based test runner, a suite of published npm packages (component testing adapters, webpack/vite dev-server integrations, plugins), and the internal tooling used to build and release all of it. Cypress is used by millions of developers to test web applications across Chrome, Firefox, Edge, WebKit, and Electron.

## Workspaces

- **`cli/`** — The main `cypress` npm package (CLI entry point) and co-located component testing framework adapters (`@cypress/react`, `@cypress/vue`, `@cypress/angular`, `@cypress/svelte`, `@cypress/mount-utils`)
- **`packages/`** — Core internal packages: the test driver, Electron app, HTTP server, proxy, launcher, frontend Vue app, launchpad, reporter, config, data-context, telemetry, types, errors, and more
- **`npm/`** — Publicly published npm packages: bundler integrations, component testing adapters, plugins, and dev tooling
- **`tooling/`** — Internal build tooling: V8 snapshot creation, `packherd` dependency bundler, and `electron-mksnapshot`
- **`system-tests/`** — Full end-to-end system test suite run against a built Cypress binary
- **`scripts/`** — Internal build, release, and CI automation scripts

## Task runbooks

Step-by-step procedures live in [`guides/`](./guides/) — start there for any multi-step workflow ([release process](./guides/release-process.md), [writing the changelog](./guides/writing-the-cypress-changelog.md), [V8 snapshots](./guides/v8-snapshots.md), and others indexed in [`guides/README.md`](./guides/README.md)). They are the canonical source for humans and agents alike.

`.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` adds a thin layer on top for the two workflows that need agent-specific execution guidance — which permissions a phase needs, long-running commands, and host quirks that would be noise in a contributor guide. Claude Code loads them on demand; **other agents should read the file directly**, since nothing loads them automatically:

- [`building-cypress-binary`](./.claude/skills/building-cypress-binary/SKILL.md) — `binary-build` / `binary-package` / `binary-zip`, non-interactive flags, `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`, macOS signing.
- [`debugging-cypress-artifacts`](./.claude/skills/debugging-cypress-artifacts/SKILL.md) — bugs that only reproduce in packaged output, the commit/build/clean/reset loop, `CYPRESS_RUN_BINARY`.

`.claude/rules/*.md` is a second thin layer, for facts that are only correct in one part of the tree — which test runner a package uses, which runtime floor a directory is bound by, how a given kind of snapshot is regenerated. Each file carries a `paths:` glob, and Claude Code loads it when it opens a matching file. They are pointers, not sources of truth: every one links back to the guide or `AGENTS.md` section that owns the topic, so **other agents can skip them** and lose nothing.

Add new guidance to a guide by default. A skill is only warranted when the content is about *running* the task rather than doing it correctly — if a contributor doing the task by hand would need to know it, it belongs in the guide. A rule is only warranted when the guidance is wrong outside a specific path. See [Choosing where guidance goes](./CONTRIBUTING.md#choosing-where-guidance-goes).

## Prerequisites

- **Node**: Use the node version specified in the `.node-version` file (check with `node -v`; run `nvm use` to manage versions)
- **Package manager**: Yarn 1 (`yarn@1.22.22`) — do not use npm or pnpm
- **Lerna**: Orchestrated via root `package.json` scripts; installed as a dev dependency
- **Electron** (for binary builds): handled automatically by `@packages/electron` during build

## Common Commands

### Setup & Development

```bash
# Install all dependencies (runs post-install hooks automatically)
yarn

# Start Cypress in dev mode (watch, rebuilds on change)
yarn dev

# Open the Cypress GUI in dev + global mode
yarn start

```

### Testing

```bash
# Run a single package's tests (go through the workspace, not the root test script —
# the root script hardcodes its own --scope flags and lerna unions them, so
# `yarn test --scope <pkg>` runs the whole default suite plus that package)
yarn workspace @packages/server test

# Target a specific vitest spec file (packages that use vitest)
yarn workspace @packages/config test -- <path-to-spec>

# Target a specific vitest spec by glob pattern
yarn workspace @packages/net-stubbing test -- "<glob-pattern>"

# Target a specific mocha spec file (packages that use mocha)
yarn workspace @packages/server test-unit -- <path-to-spec>

# Filter mocha tests by name pattern
yarn workspace @packages/server test-unit -- --grep "<pattern>"

# @packages/data-context is the one package on jest, not vitest or mocha
yarn workspace @packages/data-context test-unit -- <path-to-spec>

# Run system tests (full binary-level E2E)
yarn test-system

# Run Cypress headlessly against a specific spec (dev mode)
yarn cypress:run -- --spec "path/to/spec.cy.ts"

# Run Cypress component tests against a specific spec (dev mode)
yarn cypress:run:ct -- --spec "path/to/spec.cy.ts"
```

### Type Checking

```bash
# Type-check all TypeScript across the monorepo
yarn type-check

# Lerna-only type check pass
yarn check-ts
```

### Linting & Formatting

```bash
# Lint all packages (no bail, concurrency 2)
yarn lint

# Lint and auto-fix specific scopes
yarn lint:fix
```

> **Note**: This project does **not** use Prettier. All formatting is enforced via ESLint.

The repo is mid-migration between two ESLint configs, so ignore rules live in two places: `ignorePatterns` in the root `.eslintrc.js` for the packages still on eslintrc, and the `ignores` block in `packages/eslint-config/src/baseConfig.ts` for the packages on flat config. Build output (`cjs/`, `esm/`, `dist/`) is already ignored in both; do not add a per-package `.eslintignore` for it, since patterns in those files that contain a `/` silently match nothing. [The ESLint migration guide](./guides/eslint-migration.md#6-ignore-build-output-centrally) explains the mechanism.

### Build

```bash
# Full monorepo build
yarn build

# Build V8 snapshot (dev)
yarn build-v8-snapshot-dev

# Build V8 snapshot (prod)
yarn build-v8-snapshot-prod

# Clean all build artifacts
yarn clean

# Clean and reinstall (nuclear)
yarn clean-deps && yarn
```

## Architecture

Orientation, not a registry — the directories under `packages/`, `npm/`, and `tooling/` are the authoritative list, and each carries its own `AGENTS.md` with the detail. Read a package's own file before working in it rather than relying on the one-liner here.

### CLI & Distribution

- **`cypress` (`cli/`)** — The `cypress` npm package users install. Entry point for `cypress open`, `cypress run`, `cypress install`, etc. The published version is set by semantic-release, not by `cli/package.json` (which stays `0.0.0-development`).

### Test Runner & Driver

- **`@packages/driver`** — The JavaScript test driver that executes user test code inside the browser. Implements Cypress commands, assertions, retries, and all `cy.*` APIs.
- **`@packages/runner`** — The webpack-bundled runner UI that hosts the AUT (application under test) iframe and driver communication layer.
- **`@packages/app`** — The Vue 3 frontend for the Cypress GUI / Launchpad. Main visual interface for the desktop app.
- **`@packages/launchpad`** — Project creation, onboarding, and test file scaffold UI.
- **`@packages/frontend-shared`** — Shared Vue components and design system tokens used by `app` and `launchpad`.
- **`@packages/reporter`** — The test results reporter UI component (pass/fail tree, log panel).

### Server & Network

- **`@packages/server`** — HTTP server responsible for serving test files, handling browser launching, socket communication, and orchestrating the test run.

## Workflow Orchestration

### 1. Plan Mode Default

- Enter plan mode for ANY non-trivial task (3+ steps or architectural decisions)
- If something goes sideways, STOP and re-plan immediately - don't keep pushing
- Use plan mode for verification steps, not just building
- Write detailed specs upfront to reduce ambiguity

### 2. Subagent Strategy

- Use subagents liberally to keep main context window clean
- Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents
- For complex problems, throw more compute at it via subagents
- One task per subagent for focused execution

### 3. Self-Improvement Loop

- After ANY correction from the user: update the closest relevant `CLAUDE.md` file
- Write rules for yourself that prevent the same mistake

### 4. Verification Before Done

- Never mark a task complete without proving it works
- Diff behavior between main and your changes when relevant
- Ask yourself: "Would a staff engineer approve this?"
- Run relevant tests only, check logs, demonstrate correctness

### 5. Demand Elegance (Balanced)

- For non-trivial changes: pause and ask "is there a more elegant way?"
- If a fix feels hacky: "Knowing everything I know now, implement the elegant solution"
- Skip this for simple, obvious fixes - don't over-engineer
- Challenge your own work before presenting it

## Core Principles

- **Minimal Impact**: Changes should only touch what's necessary. Avoid introducing bugs.

## Working Constraints

- Worktrees must use a full `yarn` install in the worktree. Do not symlink `node_modules` or packages back to another checkout.
- E2E and packaged-binary integration tests do not run in the sandbox. When they are needed, provide the exact commands and ask the user to run them.
- Before committing or pushing, `yarn check-ts`, `yarn lint`, and relevant unit tests must pass locally. CI currently does not block expensive e2e jobs when these fail.

**Once you learn how to use Cypress, you can contribute in many ways:**

## Code of Conduct

All contributors are expected to abide by our [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Opening Issues

**The most important things to do are:**

- Search existing [issues](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues) for your problem.
- Understand our [roadmap](https://on.cypress.io/roadmap).
- [Update Cypress](#update-cypress).
- [Gather debugging information](#getting-more-information).
- [Fill out the provided issue template](#fill-out-our-issue-template).
- [Describe your problem, not your solution](#describe-problems)
- [Explain how to reproduce the issue](#reproducibility).

Finally, if you are up to date, supported, have collected information about the problem, and have the best reproduction instructions you can give, you are ready to [open an issue](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/new/choose).

### Update Cypress

Before filing a bug, make sure you are up to date. Your issue may have already been fixed. Even if you do not see the issue described as resolved in a newer version, a newer version may help in the process of debugging your issue by giving more helpful error messages.

[See our document on installing cypress](https://on.cypress.io/installing-cypress)

### Getting more information

For some issues, there are places you can check for more information. This may help you resolve the issue yourself. Even if it doesn't, this information can help us figure out and resolve an issue.

- For issues in the web browser, check the JavaScript console and your Network tab in your DevTools.
- Click on any command in the Command Log where the failure occurred, this will log more information about the error to the JavaScript console.
- Use Cypress [`debug`](https://on.cypress.io/debug) or [`pause`](https://on.cypress.io/pause) commands to step through your commands.
- Ask other Cypress users for help in our [chat](https://on.cypress.io/chat) or [Discord](https://on.cypress.io/discord).
- Try more advanced troubleshooting from [troubleshooting Cypress](https://on.cypress.io/debugging#Troubleshooting-Cypress) doc.

### Fill out our Issue Template

When opening an issue, there is a provided issue template. Fill out the information according to the template. This is information needed for Cypress to continue forward with your problem. Any issues that don't fill out the issue template will be closed.

### Describe Problems

When you file a feature request or bug, it's best to **describe the problem you are facing first**, not just your desired solution.

Often, your problem may have a lot in common with other similar problems. If we understand your use case, we can compare it to other use cases and sometimes find a more powerful or more general solution which solves several problems at once. Understanding the root issue can let us merge and contextualize things. Sometimes there's already a way to solve your problem that might just not be obvious.

Also, your proposed solution may not be compatible with the direction we want to take the product, but we may be able to come up with another solution which has approximately the same effect and does fit into the product direction.

### Reproducibility

**It is nearly impossible for us to resolve issues if we can not reproduce them. Your best chance of getting a bug looked at quickly is to provide a repository with a reproducible bug that can be cloned and run.**

All substantive content lives in the sibling `AGENTS.md`. This keeps `CLAUDE.md` files
minimal while making them self-documenting via the import.

---

### Codex CLI

[Docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md/) — Codex walks **downward**
from the git root to your current working directory, concatenating `AGENTS.md` files
root-first (32 KiB limit total).

`AGENTS.md` files in this repo mirror the `CLAUDE.md` list above, with the same paths
but `AGENTS.md` filename instead. The root `AGENTS.md` provides full project context;
workspace and package `AGENTS.md` files add scoped detail.

---

### Cursor

[Docs](https://cursor.com/docs/context/rules) — Cursor reads `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` and
natively reads `AGENTS.md` files.

Existing Cursor rules in this repo:

- `.cursor/BUGBOT.md` — PR review checklist (security, performance, Cypress-specific rules)
- `packages/electron/.cursor/rules/electron-upgrade.mdc` — Electron upgrade guide

| Type | Frontmatter | When active |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Always Apply | `alwaysApply: true` | Every session |
| Specific Files | `globs: ["app/**"]` | When editing a matching file |
| Agent-requested | `description: "..."` only | Agent decides based on description |
| Manual | none | Only when mentioned via `@rule-name` in chat |

---

## Why AGENTS.md Is the Single Source of Truth

Cursor and Codex read `AGENTS.md` natively; Claude Code reads it via `@import`. One edit
propagates to all three tools. The only separately-maintained content is the workflow
orchestration section in root `CLAUDE.md` — that is Claude Code-specific and intentionally
kept separate.

## Contributing

Hub contributions are preferred for canonical patterns and playbooks. Repo-local scaffolds
(`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`) should stay minimal — factual descriptions of what exists,
not aspirational guides.

If you add a new package to the monorepo, add a `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` alongside
it following the patterns in existing packages.

When repo structure, commands, or conventions change, update the relevant `AGENTS.md` /
`CLAUDE.md` files in the same PR (similar to keeping READMEs accurate).

report.overview: Cypress is a browser testing platform for developers running end-to-end and component tests locally or in CI. This monorepo combines the installable CLI and Node API, an Electron application, a browser-side command driver, Vue interfaces, and framework/bundler integrations. At commit 7d987f04740f8f5388ac3116e8ef7957373ead14, distinctive implementation details include shared interception logic across HTTP-proxy and Chromium CDP transports, GraphQL application state, and CLI attachment to existing interactive sessions.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to Cypress at commit 7d987f04740f8f5388ac3116e8ef7957373ead14 on develop. Treat this brief as a bounded source investigation, not exhaustive repository coverage or proof that tests pass. The investigation read public source, tests, manifests, configuration, and CI definitions without executing repository code, installing dependencies, making network requests, or writing files. Preserve those restrictions if continuing this audit. Use rtk proxy for raw read-only shell commands, and cite exact tracked files with line anchors from the pinned commit. Never read credentials, keys, or .env files.

Begin with root AGENTS.md and the nearest package AGENTS.md, then inspect the relevant package manifest and actual implementation. Cypress has several runtime boundaries: the CLI runs in the user's Node; the main application runs in Electron; configuration and setupNodeEvents run in a child using the resolved user Node; the driver executes in the browser. Check cli/package.json engines before introducing runtime APIs into CLI or config-child paths. Yarn 1 and Lerna organize the workspaces. New source and fixtures use TypeScript, single quotes, two spaces, no semicolons, and ESLint formatting.

For execution changes, follow cli/lib/bin/cypress.ts into CLI.init, exec/run.ts, and exec/spawn.ts. The CLI verifies the installed binary unless dev mode is selected, decorates arguments with cwd and user Node details, and launches another process. On the server, lib/cypress.ts selects a mode; lib/modes/index.ts initializes DataContext; modes/run.ts opens the project, selects the browser, executes specs, aggregates results, runs lifecycle hooks, and writes public output. Programmatic cypress.run reads that output from a temporary JSON file.

For interception changes, read driver/src/cy/net-stubbing/add-command.ts and events/index.ts, net-stubbing server driver-events.ts, middleware/request.ts, handle-intercept-request.ts, and handle-intercept-response.ts. Matching and policy rules belong in network-interception; transport effects belong in adapters. Middleware routes precede ordinary routes, whose order is reversed. ServerBase owns one shared stubbing state across runtime changes. Preserve both CDP Fetch and HTTP-proxy behavior, including forceHttp1 coverage.

For session changes, read cypress-sessions/lib/index.ts, server/lib/cypress-sessions.ts, project-base.ts, routes.ts, and CLI cypress-sessions modules. Interactive sessions persist immutable identity through serialized temporary-file writes and atomic rename. Browser attachment stays in memory and is obtained through a session-id probe; the CLI also checks process liveness and CDP reachability before selecting a ready session.

Application mutations belong under DataContext.actions. GraphQL schema and consumer types are generated; adapter artifacts copied into cli are generated too. Edit their owners rather than generated output. The server mixes Mocha and Vitest, the CLI uses Vitest, and data-context uses Jest. In an execution-authorized implementation task, choose a narrow workspace test first, then relevant type/lint and browser or system checks. Report actual outcomes separately from test existence. Review privileged commands, file paths, configuration IPC, origin gates, and transport switching as trust boundaries; source observations alone do not establish vulnerabilities.

system_map.summary: The system spans a user-Node CLI, an Electron main process, a configuration/plugin child process, and browser bundles. The application exposes GraphQL and browser communication services while coordinating projects and network interception. Distribution includes an npm module and platform-specific desktop binaries, with separate build and release machinery.

claims.claim: Yarn workspaces cover cli, packages, npm, tooling, system-tests, and scripts; Lerna uses the same package layout and selects Yarn as its npm client.
The executable entry calls CLI.init(); the module entry exports open, run, cli, defineConfig, and defineComponentFramework.
Server startup installs the require hook before loading start-cypress; runElectron dispatches directly to modes when already inside Electron and otherwise opens an Electron child.
ProjectConfigIpc forks configuration code with cwd at the config file's directory and execPath set to the resolved user Node; cli/package.json supports Node ^22, ^24, or >=26.
The Vue application uses generated hash-history routes; its state backend builds a Nexus GraphQL schema with DataContext as context and a wrapped remote schema.
createProxyRuntime and createCdpFetchRuntime compose interception transports; both receive the server-owned NetStubbingState rather than creating independent route state.
Inspected local storage includes versioned binary caches, project/global state.json files, and PID-named interactive-session records; these serve different lifecycle owners.

Root build runs the Lerna build, Electron binary build, and CLI build; release documentation distinguishes independently published @cypress packages from desktop binaries promoted in S3 and the cypress npm artifact.

feature_catalog.summary: The inspected user surfaces include terminal execution, the Node API, interactive spec management, component mounting, network interception, and Cypress Cloud integration. The tap command adds discovery and control of an existing open-mode session. This catalogue groups evidenced capabilities; the bounded inspection does not enumerate every cy command, UI component, or published integration.

claims.claim: cypress run exposes E2E/component selection, browser and spec filtering, config overrides, reporters, headed/headless operation, recording, parallel groups, cancellation thresholds, and POSIX exit codes.

cypress open supports project/global mode, testing-type selection, browser/config overrides, and detached launch; install, verify, cache, version, and info provide installation and diagnostic operations.

The Node API provides open() and run(); run() returns parsed run output or a structured failed result when the binary produces no readable results. defineConfig() and defineComponentFramework() return their input objects.
The Specs page presents a spec list or no-specs state, opens CreateSpecModal, and subscribes to spec changes; Settings queries configuration and subscribes to configChange.
cy.intercept accepts URL, method/URL, or matcher-object overloads and function, string-body, or static-response handlers; middleware requires a function handler.

React mount() clears the previous root, creates a ReactDOM root, and delegates to makeMountFn; the CLI exports React, Vue, Angular, and Svelte adapters, while the Vite dev-server integration resolves project Vite and warms support/spec modules conditionally.
Cloud-facing features include login/signup and viewer validation, recorded/parallel run orchestration, and a Runs page that selects Git-tree or project runs and refetches after connectivity returns.

cypress tap accepts session PID, JSON output, and timeout options; CLI-owned subcommands include sessions, status, specs, run, dom, aria, and inspect, with browser driving limited to Chromium-family sessions.

data_flow.summary: Inputs cross explicit boundaries through CLI argument translation, configuration IPC, GraphQL operations, and network-event frames. State is split between DataContext, browser route/command state, server interception state, and local persistence. Outputs include browser responses, UI subscriptions, JSON run results, process exit codes, and session discovery records.

claims.claim: processRunOptions translates user options into binary flags, including --run-project, config/env, recording key, reporter, and specs; spawn.start adds cwd, userNodePath, and userNodeVersion.
Configuration crosses into a child as project/config arguments and inherited environment; RunPlugins sends modified setupConfig and event registrations back through setupTestingType:reply.
GraphQL socket requests parse JSON and query text, execute graphqlSchema with a request context, return results through a callback, and balance DataContext active-request accounting in finally.

The driver annotates regex/glob matchers for transport, lowercases header matcher names, stores handlers locally by routeId, and emits route:added; the server restores matcher types and appends BackendRoute to state.routes.

Matching excludes component dev-server paths and can synthesize preflight responses; matchRoutes orders middleware first, ordinary handlers in reverse registration order, and excludes disabled routes.

Interception buffers request/response bodies, preserves binary content, exchanges subscription events with browser handlers, merges changes, and either ends a stubbed request or continues transport with a modified body stream.

Interactive-session JSON holds schema, PID, resolved project root, port, session ID, and testing type; CDP/browser attachment remains in memory, while the probe reads machine/user identity at request time.

runSpecs aggregates per-spec statistics, transforms results with createPublicRunResults, invokes after:run, and writes output; programmatic run() supplies a temporary output path and reads that JSON after the child finishes.

behavior_traces.summary: Three concrete flows were followed across their relevant files: test-run startup/results, interception registration through response completion, and interactive-session persistence through CLI attachment. The traces below retain important branches such as dev verification bypass, recording delegation, static-response termination, and browser-readiness filtering. A supplementary startup trace explains how the interactive window becomes available.

claims.claim: Run entry: bin/cypress.ts → CLI.init() → run command action → runModule.start() → processRunOptions() → spawnStart(); non-dev execution awaits binary verify.start(), while dev execution bypasses it.

Run initialization: cypress.start() parses argv and selects run for runProject → startInMode() → runElectron() → modes factory → setCtx(makeDataContext()) and initializeMode() → modes/run.run() awaits loading and calls ready().

Run completion: ready() discovers browsers and opens the project, validates recording parameters, and handles empty specs; runAllSpecs() calls runSpecs(), which invokes before:run → iterateThroughSpecs/runEachSpec → runSpec() → after:run → writeOutput(). Recording delegates through createRunAndRecordSpecs; POSIX mode collapses failure counts except reserved code 112.

Intercept registration: addCommand() installs intercept → getMatcherOptions() → validateRouteMatcherOptions() → addRoute() → emitNetEvent('route:added') via Cypress.backend('net', ...) → onNetStubbingEvent() → onRouteAdded().

Intercept request: SetMatchingRoutes() applies dev-server/preflight conditions and core.matchRoutes() → InterceptRequest() → core.handleRequest() → handleInterceptRequest() creates and registers InterceptedRequest → ensureBody() → addDefaultSubscriptions() → before:request handlers → merge changes → end() if responseSent, otherwise continueRequest().

Intercept response: handleInterceptResponse() bypasses unmatched requests, obtains a plain-text/binary body, invokes before:response → response:callback → response subscriptions, merges response/header changes, and continues with getBodyStream(); response finish emits after:response and removes the request from server state.

Session lifecycle: ProjectBase registers an open-mode session → addSession() creates UUID identity → persist() serializes writes and renames a temporary JSON file → CLI readLiveSessions() validates records/reaps dead PIDs → verifySessionRecord() checks the session echo and CDP /json/version → resolveSession() filters ready supported sessions → CDP attachment probes page targets for the tap binding.

Interactive startup: modes factory starts initializeMode() → interactive.run() concurrently awaits app.whenReady() and makeGraphQLServer() → ready() loads saved state and opens the desktop window → optional 'Cypress is ready' sentinel lets detached CLI spawning destroy streams, unref the child, and resolve.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; their existence is not a passing result. The repository combines Vitest, Mocha, Jest, Cypress browser suites, and a system-test harness. Inspected coverage includes option translation, session persistence/probing, subscription behavior, configuration child failures, and browser interception. The inventory and test inspection are bounded, so local TODOs and mocks describe specific limits rather than whole-repository coverage gaps.

claims.claim: Root Vitest discovers package/tooling/script project configurations and the CLI project, excludes system-tests, and configures V8 coverage plus default/JUnit reporting; server test-unit runs Mocha then Vitest, while data-context uses Jest with experimental VM modules.

CLI run tests assert project-path rejection, conflicting headed/headless flags, testing-type choices, and POSIX argument forwarding; verify/spawn are mocked, so these tests do not establish real binary launch behavior.

Server session tests use temporary cache directories and inspect actual JSON files, covering immutable identity, temporary-file cleanup, swallowed write failure, pending-write removal, and project-switch preservation.

CLI session tests exercise fake HTTP sessions and closed ports, asserting rejection of recycled-port/session mismatches, malformed JSON, timeout, and stale CDP endpoints while retaining browser identity.
InterceptedRequest Vitest tests resolve pending handlers through a mocked socket and assert enabled/disabled subscription dispatch counts; they do not exercise a real proxy or CDP transport.

The driver interception suite asserts route state and backend event frames in browser tests, but declares 15 retries and unique route names for documented flakiness/request leakage. runEachSpec also carries an explicit TODO for a cancelled just-in-time component-run system test.

A Jest ProjectConfigIpc test loads a real configuration child and injects EPIPE; system config tests cover invalid settings and JS/TS config filenames, and the harness offers withBinary mode. A config-spec TODO requests environment-variable coverage locally.

Inspected CircleCI definitions gate contributor builds behind approval, select suites through pipeline parameters, add Chrome forceHttp1 smoke coverage, and aggregate browser/system/type/lint checks at ready-to-release; GitHub Actions separately checks semantic PR titles/changelog and generates release SBOMs.

risk_map.summary: These are source observations and explicitly marked hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Sensitive boundaries include configuration execution, privileged browser-to-server commands, filesystem access, GraphQL listeners, and CDP session control. Transport switching and V8 snapshot composition create substantial coupling. Runtime validation and broader test results remain unknown because this investigation executed no repository code.

claims.claim: Configuration/plugin execution is a host-code boundary: ProjectConfigIpc inherits most process environment and forks with the user Node, while RunPlugins calls setupNodeEvents and later invokes registered handlers.

PrivilegedCommandsManager validates channel keys and command name/args for E2E requests before dispatching env, file, origin, and task operations; hasVerifiedCommand uses find() without removing the entry despite its removal comment.

readFile/writeFile resolve caller paths against projectRoot without a containment check in those helpers; absolute paths or parent traversal can therefore address locations outside the project. Whether a caller is authorized depends on upstream command controls.

Hypothesis for focused review: the Launchpad GraphQL listener supplies no explicit bind host and accepts requests without Origin; its CORS denial controls browser response visibility rather than being an authentication check. Actual reachability and exploitability were not tested.

Session probes expose live CDP URL and machine/user identity when the URL session ID matches; session identity is persisted under the cache. The project server binds loopback, and CLI probes additionally require matching identity and reachable CDP, making local record/endpoint access a sensitive boundary.

Transport switching must preserve the same stubbing-state object and publish mode/runtime consistently; server comments identify broken intercept matching and disagreement with the still-running browser as failure modes.
cy.exec's server module remains imported solely for V8 snapshot composition and throws a Cypress 16 removal error; deleting this apparently obsolete stub has a documented mksnapshot failure risk.

A successful production-build command alone does not prove type correctness: server build-prod and data-context build-prod explicitly tolerate tsc failure, while separate check-ts scripts enforce no-emit checks.

extension_points.summary: Public customization is concentrated in Cypress command registration, setupNodeEvents, component adapters, and CLI APIs. Internal extension seams include injected network ports, ordered policies, generated frontend routes, and Nexus schema plugins. New code should enter through the owning seam because transport, generated-artifact, and process boundaries constrain implementation placement.

claims.claim: Cypress.Commands supports add/addAll, overwrite, and addQuery; registration protects built-in/reserved names and derives parent/child/dual command behavior from prevSubject.

setupNodeEvents receives registerChildEvent and initialConfig; event registrations are validated, repeated task registrations merge, and a default file preprocessor is installed only when the user supplies none.
Plugin execution dispatch has specific wrappers for dev-server:start, file:preprocessor, browser launch, tasks, and run/spec/screenshot lifecycle events.

NetworkInterceptionCore accepts injected policy, request/response, document preparation, capture, cookie, command-log, and browser-automation ports; effects are delegated rather than embedded in matching logic.
NetworkPolicyRegistry.add appends policies; runPolicies filters by phase and when(exchange), applies policies sequentially with shared state, and stops after end().
Frontend pages plug into virtual:generated-pages and generated layouts; createRouter adds default-page redirection and installs the Studio unsaved-changes navigation guard.
GraphQL extension uses schemaTypes, remote-schema merging, and structural/runtime Nexus plugins; mutations and filesystem writes are intended to run through DataContext.actions.

Component integration offers defineComponentFramework and a devServer contract returning port/close; tap has an ordered CLI command registry that precedes commands advertised by the running session's schema.

agent_handoff.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and no repository files were changed. Future implementation work should start from package-local guidance and identify the runtime, generated artifacts, and test runner before editing. The highest-value boundaries to preserve are shared interception state, session identity/persistence, user-Node configuration execution, and public CLI/module compatibility. This is a bounded investigation rather than exhaustive inventory or verification.

claims.claim: Read root/package AGENTS.md and the appropriate guides before implementation; package documentation supplies architecture and runner details, and canonical multi-step workflows belong in guides.
Use Yarn 1 and existing workspace scripts; avoid root yarn test --scope for narrowing because its hardcoded Lerna scopes broaden the run.
Identify the runtime before using APIs: CLI/config-child support follows cli engines, the main process follows Electron, and browser bundles have a separate browser floor.
New code and fixtures use TypeScript and ESLint conventions; preserve single quotes, no semicolons, two-space indentation, type-only imports, and documented skip reasons.

Edit CT adapter sources under npm rather than copied cli artifacts; regenerate Nexus/schema outputs through data-context build, and rebuild the shared session contract before CLI consumers pick up changes.

For execution-authorized validation, target CLI Vitest files with yarn workspace cypress test-unit -- <spec>, server Mocha with test-unit-mocha, server Vitest with test-unit-vitest, and data-context Jest with test-unit -- <spec>; then run relevant check-ts/lint scripts. These commands were inspected, not run in this audit.

Keep platform-dependent CLI tests host-independent: mock both os.arch and the arch package, avoid regenerating canonical snapshots to hide host drift, and account for util._cachedArch singleton state.

Interception edits require both browser-CDP and forceHttp1 validation plans; preserve the server-owned state across browser switches, and treat contributor CI approval/parameter filters as execution conditions rather than proof that all suites ran.
